newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany welcomes presidential hopeful Lebed.
newsitem.headline: Germany welcomes presidential hopeful Lebed.

text.p: Russian presidential hopeful Alexander Lebed got a warm reception in Bonn on Wednesday from a German establishment with which he said he wanted to do business.

The gravel-voiced retired paratroop general, making only his third visit outside the former Soviet Union, has come to Russia's biggest creditor and supporter in the West aiming to make himself known as a potential successor to Boris Yeltsin.

"Germany must look at me, I need to look at Germany, we have to decide whether we should work together or not. I hope that we come to the conclusion that we should work together," Lebed told Reuters Television on the second day of his five-day visit.

Lebed, who came a strong third in a presidential election last June and briefly served as Yeltsin's security adviser, has not concealed the fact that he believes Yeltsin should quit because of his continuing ill health and allow a new election.
On Wednesday, before a two-hour closed-door meeting with German political and economic experts, he was moderating his tone and stressing his respect for the electoral process.

"The Russian people made their choice last year, the president was elected. Now he's become rather ill. We all hope he recovers. I'm gearing up for a long-term task, tough and exhausting work. It won't be a simple or easy process."
Germany's body politic was giving Lebed, in protocol terms only a private citizen, at least four-star treatment in granting him meetings with parliamentary leaders of all major parties.
The programme was similar to a visit last year by communist leader Gennady Zyuganov, then a declared presidential candidate.
While Chancellor Helmut Kohl's powerful lieutenant Wolfgang Schaeuble declined to pose for photographs with Zyuganov, he had no such scruples with Lebed and gave him a friendly welcome.
The German Foreign Policy Association (DGAP), which invited Lebed, said industrialists were impressed after dining with him.

"Lebed is bringing the message that he will be president, he is 100 percent convinced of that, but that German and Western European industrialists need not fear his policies," DGAP Russia expert Alexander Rahr told German radio.

"Lebed relies greatly on charisma, and the many industry bosses who had dinner with him came away very satisfied...(The most important message is) the West will be able to have some kind of influence on him and his policies," Rahr said.
Lebed did, however, come close to repeating comments in a magazine interview last year which unnerved many Germans.
Asked by the Sueddeutsche Zeitung if he was a democrat, Lebed replied "No".

"You should know that there is no democracy in Russia. We have an authoritarian regime. Look at our constitution...You have to change people's mentality and consciousness, create the legal basis," said Lebed, a conservative who says he favours a "dictatorship of law'.
"Perhaps one day I will become a democratic politician, but I say honestly that I'll need time to absorb it all," he added, according to an advance release from Thursday's edition.
There were no plans for Lebed to meet Kohl, Russia's leading advocate in its attempts to join Western economic and political structures. Lebed said he understood the reasons for this.

"The official figures here have close ties to official figures in Russia," he said. "It would have been tactless for them to invite me or for me to try to insist. The time isn't right now, but the time will come for us to meet."
Lebed arrived in Bonn on Tuesday and had a busy schedule of political meetings stretching into Thursday.
He is due to travel to Duesseldorf on Thursday evening for a speech to industrialists, and on Friday will meet the Bavarian state premier, Edmund Stoiber, in Munich.
